label: A friend
blurb: A current or former close friend.

intro.title: Stepping away from a friend
body: Friend breakups are real breakups, and there’s usually less language and less support for them. Many people feel awkward even admitting how much it hurts.
This path helps you work out what you actually want, choose how to do it, and handle the group, the guilt, and the loneliness afterwards.

questions.title: What is still tied together?
questions.help: Pick any that apply. It changes which steps you see.

options.label: We share a friend group or community
We live together or share a space
One of us owes the other money, or has the other’s things

expect.title: It can hurt as much as a romantic breakup
expect.body: Grief for a friendship is real, and it isn’t overreacting.

expect.title: They may not take it well
expect.body: Some people respond with hurt, anger, or promises to change. You can be kind and still hold your decision.

expect.title: Mutual friends may feel caught in the middle
expect.body: Not everyone will handle it well. Try not to make anyone choose.

expect.title: Guilt and second thoughts
expect.body: Choosing your own wellbeing isn’t selfish. Second thoughts don’t cancel your reasons.

expect.title: Loneliness
expect.body: Missing someone is not an instruction to go back. It’s a signal to look after yourself and your other connections.

steps.title: If this friend is controlling or threatening
steps.summary: A calm, honest talk isn’t always safe. Choose a method that protects you first.
how: Skip the face-to-face conversation. A brief written message, or simply stepping back, is safer.
Keep a copy of anything you send and anything they send back.
Tell someone you trust. Avoid shared spaces and keep your accounts and location private.
Use the Safety page and, if you feel in danger, call your local emergency number.

steps.title: Work out whether this is a drift or a rift
steps.summary: A drift is when nothing bad happened and you’ve grown apart. A rift is when a specific hurt did the damage. What you do next depends on which it is.
how: Journal about how you feel afterwards: drained, resentful, or lighter?
Look at the pattern. Is it one bad stretch or a long habit?
Talk to a trusted friend, who may spot things you’ve missed.
Decide what you actually want: take a break, see them less, or end it.

steps.title: Choose how you’ll do it
steps.summary: There are three honest ways. Pick the one that fits the person and the situation.
how: A direct conversation, in person at a neutral place with few distractions, gives the most closure.
A short written message is better if emotions run high or you fear their reaction. Keep it brief, and keep a copy.
Fading out slowly is gentler, and leaves them without closure.
Ghosting leaves the least closure and can be confusing and hurtful. It can be justified if they’re toxic or unsafe.

steps.title: Navigate the friend group
steps.summary: Don’t make mutual friends pick sides.
how: Don’t badmouth them to the group. It tends to come back around.
Keep one-on-one time with the friends who matter to you.
Mute group chats rather than making a scene.
Skip events they’ll be at for a while, or go for a short time with a buddy.
Accept that some friendships may cool, and let it be okay.

scripts.label: To a mutual friend
scripts.text: I’m taking some distance from them. I don’t want to put you in the middle, so I won’t ask you to take sides. I’d like us to keep seeing each other.

steps.title: Settle borrowed things and money once
steps.summary: Debts and belongings are a common reason a break doesn’t stay broken.
how: Make a list of what each of you has of the other’s.
Return items through a third party or a drop-off, at an agreed time, in writing.
For money, agree a clear plan in writing, or decide to let it go.
Keep it brief and written. Don’t use it as a reason to chat.

steps.title: If you share a home
steps.summary: You can’t avoid each other completely, so set simple rules for the space.
how: Agree to keep talk to practical matters, in writing where possible.
Set quiet hours and a schedule for shared spaces.
Look at your lease: subletting, moving out, or a mediator through a community mediation service.
Pick a realistic move date and begin planning.

steps.title: If you work or study together
steps.summary: Professional only: polite, brief, and about the work.
how: Keep contact to work topics and work channels.
Be courteous, skip personal chat, and avoid being alone with them if you’re uneasy.
If it becomes harassment, document it and tell a manager or HR.

scripts.label: Keeping it professional
scripts.text: Happy to work on this together. I’d rather keep us to work topics.

steps.title: Say it clearly and kindly
steps.summary: A kind, clear message is easier to stick to than a vague one.
how: Start with what you valued, then say the issue.
Use “I” statements and be specific. Describe your experience, not their flaws.
Avoid “it’s not you, it’s me”. It can sound dismissive.
Say plainly what you want: less contact, a break, or an end.
Finish kindly, and don’t promise more than you mean.

scripts.label: Starting a direct conversation
scripts.text: I value our friendship, and that’s why I want to be honest. I’ve noticed I often feel drained after we spend time together, and I need to step back.

scripts.label: A written message
scripts.text: I’ve thought about this a lot. I’m going to step back from our friendship. I’m grateful for the good times and I wish you well. I won’t be replying to messages for now.

scripts.label: A clean break
scripts.text: I’ve decided to end our friendship. I’m not looking to argue about it. I wish you all the best.

steps.title: Handle their reaction
steps.summary: You can be compassionate and still not change your mind.
how: Let them speak without interrupting, and acknowledge their feelings without agreeing.
If they promise to change, ask whether it addresses the core issue, and whether you believe it.
Calmly repeat your decision. You don’t have to win the argument.
You can end the conversation any time.

scripts.label: When they promise to change
scripts.text: I appreciate you saying that. Ultimately, I need space, and my decision stays the same.

steps.title: Sort out social media
how: Mute or unfollow if you honestly won’t look. Block if you will.
Don’t post vague or pointed content about them, and don’t reply to theirs.
Review who can see your posts and what you’re tagged in.
If they harass you, screenshot it before blocking.

steps.title: When they reach out
steps.summary: A friend may try an apology, a nudge through others, or guilt. Use a plan, not a feeling.
how: If you’re not ready, no reply is fine.
If you reply, one calm sentence that repeats your decision.
Look for whether they’re addressing the actual issue, or just wanting things back to normal.
Log the contact.

scripts.label: A short reply
scripts.text: Thanks for reaching out. I meant what I said, and I’m not ready for contact.

steps.title: Don’t let guilt pull you back
steps.summary: Looking after your wellbeing isn’t selfish.
how: Name it: “this is guilt, not new information.”
Read your reasons.
Don’t let pressure or manipulation drag you back.
Talk it through with someone on your side.

steps.title: If they gossip or retaliate
steps.summary: Some people lash out. Stay out of it.
how: Don’t defend yourself publicly or retaliate. Rumors usually fade faster without feeding them.
Screenshot harassment and keep a record.
Tell a couple of trusted people what’s going on, so you’re not carrying it alone.
If there are threats or you fear for your safety, use the Safety page and report it.

steps.title: Look after the loneliness
steps.summary: Missing a friend is normal and it doesn’t mean you should go back.
how: Schedule social time each week, even something small.
Reconnect with people you’ve drifted from.
Join something regular: a class, a group, a team.
Lean on a “backup” person for the moments you feel the pull.

steps.title: Allow the grief
steps.summary: Losing a friendship deserves the same kindness as any other loss.
how: Don’t minimize it because “it’s just a friend”.
Write about what the friendship gave you, and what it cost.
Let yourself be sad without letting sadness make decisions.

steps.title: Decide whether the door is open or closed
steps.summary: Both are fine. Just be honest about which one.
how: If you want to leave it open, choose a time to reassess, such as a year, and don’t keep checking before then.
If you want it closed, say so clearly and respectfully.
Remember the old issues may return. You may need to end it again.

steps.title: Decide what you want from friendships
steps.summary: Use what you learned to choose better, not to withdraw.
how: Write down what a good friend does, and what you want to do differently.
Notice early signs: one-sided effort, put-downs, pressure, secrecy.
Put your energy into friendships that feel reciprocal.
